parts:
Dr. Reinhold:

Seven years worth of data are great. It would be good to know how the data
would look if put into a spreadsheet, or modeled as a plain analysis of
variance but first I'd like to know more about the between observer
variability. Even with different observers, over time the variance should
tend toward stabilizing. If not, some type of tranform might be helpful
stabilize the variance and meet stat requirements. If you can get some
stability and almost meet other requirements, you might then see how best
to account for the error variance by some type of stratification or
covariance.
Please tell us more about the data, when it was collected, how often, and

so on. Please tell us if your primary focus is on estimations as they vary
by seasons or other factors. Also, are there any secondary measures, like
foliage eaten or destroyed, or carcasses, or droppings, etc, or other
studies that we should know about?

Gary King at the Institute for Quantitative Studies at Harvard has written
software, free to download, like Amelia (http://gking.harvard.edu/amelia)
and zelig (http://projects.iq.harvard.edu/zelig) that do good work on
missing values of different types. Send him an email, describing what data

you have and see what he suggests.

From the Amelia webpage:

Amelia II "multiply imputes" missing data in a single cross-section (such
as a survey), from a time series (like variables collected for each year in
a country), or from a time-series-cross-sectional data set (such as
collected by years for each of several countries).Amelia II implements our
bootstrapping-based algorithm that gives essentially the same answers as
the standard IP or EMis approaches, is usually considerably faster than
existing approaches and can handle many more variables. Unlike Amelia I and
other statistically rigorous imputation software, it virtually never

crashes (but please let us know if you find to the contrary!). The program
also generalizes existing approaches by allowing for trends in time series
across observations within a cross-sectional unit, as well as priors that
allow experts to incorporate beliefs they have about the values of missing
cells in their data. Amelia II also includes useful diagnostics of the fit
of multiple imputation models. The program works from the R command line or
via a graphical user interface that does not require users to know R.
Amelia is named after this famous missing person.

Multiple imputation involves imputing *m* values for each missing cell in
your data matrix and creating *m* "completed" data sets. (Across these
completed data sets, the observed values are the same, but the missing
values are filled in with different imputations that reflect our
uncertainty about the missing data.) After imputation, Amelia will then
save the *m* data sets. You then apply whatever statistical method you
would have used if there had been no missing values to each of the *m* data
sets, and use a simple procedure to combine the results. Under normal
circumstances, you only need to impute once and can then analyze the
*m* imputed
data sets as many times and for as many purposes as you wish. The advantage
of Amelia is that it combines the comparative speed and ease-of-use of our
algorithm with the power of multiple imputation, to let you focus on your
substantive research questions rather than spending time developing complex
application-specific models for nonresponse in each new data set. Unless
the rate of missingness is exceptionally high, *m=5* (the program default)
will usually be adequate. Other methods of dealing with missing data, such
as listwise deletion, mean substitution, or single imputation, are in
common circumstances biased, inefficient, or both. When multiple imputation
works properly, it fills in data in such a way as to not change any
relationships in the data but which enables the inclusion of all the
observed data in the partially missing rows."
and some references for free download:

- Papers related to Amelia:
- James Honaker and Gary King, "What to do About Missing Values in
Time Series Cross-Section
Data<http://gking.harvard.edu/files/abs/pr-abs.shtml>
" *American Journal of Political Science* Vol. 54, No. 2 (April,
2010): Pp. 561-581. Article PDF<http://gking.harvard.edu/files/pr.pdf>
- Gary King, James Honaker, Anne Joseph, and Kenneth Scheve. "Analyzing
Incomplete Political Science Data: An Alternative Algorithm for Multiple
Imputation <http://gking.harvard.edu/publications/view/3710>",*American
Political Science Review*, Vol. 95, No. 1 (March, 2001): Pp. 49-69.
evil.pdf <http://gking.harvard.edu/files/gking/files/evil.pdf>
- Matthew Blackwell, James Honaker, and Gary King. *Multiple
Overimputation: A Unified Approach to Measurement Error and
Missing Data<http://gking.harvard.edu/publications/view/6388>
*, 2010.measure.pdf<http://gking.harvard.edu/files/gking/files/measure.pdf>
- A short course video <http://vimeo.com/18534025>circa 1999 which
James, Ann, and Ken gave some years ago that explains mulitiple imputation
in general, and the innovation in Amelia I in particular. Viewers will need
to impute about 10 minutes of the video (at 10:19), which might have been
when we reported the location of Ms. Earhart's plane.
There's a good discussion list on Amelia and missing values, subscription
is free <https://lists.gking.harvard.edu/mailman/listinfo/amelia> and

asking questions to the entire list is by emailing the list
ame...@lists.gking.harvard.edu.

Please keep us informed on your progress.

Dwight Hines

messages.author: 778abaa663647a33
messages.subject: Re: Incomplete detection on line: terrestrial methods
parts:
Linda-

From the description of your survey and data, the removal configuration
would be the best alternative for a dual-observer survey. However, it is
not an optimal design due to the assumption that detection probability is
the same for both observers. You can use covariates for differences like
aural vs visual detections but only if the reason they call is independent
of distance. You can include a covariate for each pair of observers but
unless you have lots of data for each pair, it is unlikely you will fit a
model with a separate term for each pair. I've been developing random
effect models which I plan to extend to dual-observer survey data and this
might work for your situation with many observer (pairs).

With regards to your various species, it is essential to remember that dual
observer surveys are largely ineffective at handling availability bias
(like being underground). Also, if "scarper" means animals are moving
before being detected that will not be handled with the dual observer
survey and will likely create negative bias. Regardless of the issues, I'd
recommend implementing the removal configuration as long as it is not too
difficult in the field.

regards --jefff

Jeff and Dwight,
Thanks for your replies, very helpful.

Some more info:
The data was collected from 2006 onwards, and is continuing, annually. W=
e try for the same time of year but it happens anywhere between April and=
September, depending on weather and boat availability. The project is f=
or a federal grant - we have to get population estimates each year. Howe=
ver, the populations fluctuate substantially in response to rainfall - no=
t necessarily seasonal, but depends if it's a drought. So an annual popu=
lation estimate is really a snapshot resulting from the preceding rainfal=
l. Ultimately we're working out if we can predict by rainfall when the p=
opulations will be at their height, and therefore when to take animals of=
f for translocation.

There are no secondary measures, except for grid trapping we've done in e=
arlier years, but for the smaller species. We are doing spotlighting to =
compare populations with similar surveys done 20 years ago. We are bound=
by the grant to do spotlighting this way, but for future years I would l=
ike to see the stats more robust. I'm hoping this year we can just get a=
n idea of what we've been missing with unseen animals on the line. I wil=
l have a go at the removal configuration on our upcoming trip in June.

The bettongs make their call in response to our presence, as they are ala=
rmed and hop away. Sometimes the rufous hare-wallabies also make a disti=
nctive alarm cry. The other two species are quiet.
Yes, scarper means hopping away because they hear us coming through the t=
hick veg. But in the thick veg, we may be unlikely to see them anyway, e=
ven if they stay put.

Linda

Date: Fri, 15 Feb 2013 12:01:52 +0800

nh...@DEC.WA.GOV.AU>>
Subject: Incomplete detection on line: terrestrial methods

Dear Distance,

We spotlight along transects for four species of ground-dwelling marsupia=
l on two islands off the west coast of Australia. Can anyone give me adv=

ice on what we should be doing about missing animals on the line?

Details:

Most of the habitat is open, but for the patches of dense bush, the anima=
ls would be able to hear us coming and scarper before we get to them. Som=
etimes we do see animals in the dense vegetation. One of our species, th=
e burrowing bettong, often makes a distinctive sound so if we don't see i=
t, we know what it is. For the other three species, or for burrowing bett=
ongs that don't make the call, we hear animals rustling under dense bushe=
s but we don't know what they are because we can't see them, so they are =
missed. For burrowing bettongs, 21% of sightings are because we hear them=
first. There is only 3% of the other species that we hear first. The s=
potlighter who walks in front often misses heard-first animals (the navig=
ator walks behind and also looks for animals).

(From separate radio-tracking data of the western barred bandicoots, they=
were pretty well active for the first half of the night (which is when w=
e spotlight), and they have a rest period during the latter half of the n=
ight. We have to assume that all four species are active during the entir=
e first half of the night (and not down their burrows/resting under bushe=
s.)

I've been reading the "Methods for incomplete detection at distance zero"=
chapter in the Advanced Distance Sampling book. Should I be gathering da=
ta for the "Removal configuration"? We have never done this before, and e=
ach time we survey we have different volunteers and staff, generally with=
a lot of between-observer variability.

What does all this mean for the data we have gathered in the last seven y=
ears? Should we keep swapping roles as we walk and note which sightings w=
ere missed by the first observer from now on? Does it matter that we woul=
d not satisfy the equality assumption because we use both visual and acou=
stic detection?
Our observers could walk side-by side through some habitat, but single-fi=

le when we have to clamber through the thick veg.

Thank you in anticipation,
